newsitem.title: HONG KONG: British rebuff China call for early PLA deployment.
newsitem.headline: British rebuff China call for early PLA deployment.

text.p: China got a swift rebuff from Britain on Thursday when it demanded the People's Liberation Army enter Hong Kong before the formal sovereignty transfer so soldiers can be in position by midnight June 30.
"There is no question of Britain agreeing (to this)," a Foreign Office spokesman declared, as the British garrison insisted it alone remains responsible till the handover in 19 days' time.

The clash deepened a handover rift between Britain and China after the London government, along with Washington, decided to boycott the inauguration of an unelected provisional legislature to replace Hong Kong's democratically elected parliament.

China says it needs a few hours before the midnight handover to deploy its main force. It has already sent an advance party of 200 soldiers to prepare garrison, supply and communications facilities. Britain insisted they be unarmed and wear uniforms only in barracks.
For China, the PLA's arrival will be the most important visible symbol of its restored sovereignty over the territory it lost to Britain in the 19th century opium trade wars.

But many of Hong Kong's 6.4 million people view the PLA with alarm because of its "butcher image" over the communist army's bloody crackdown on student-led democracy protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989.

Beijing-controlled newspapers quoted China's official spokesman in Hong Kong, Zhang Junsheng, as saying: "The People's Liberation Army should be in Hong Kong barracks before the zero hour on July 1 so that after the completion of the handover ceremony they can take up defence responsibilities."
His statement to Ta Kung Pao and Wen Wei Po was the latest sign that China is harrying Britain behind the scenes over the timing of the future PLA garrison's entry on to Hong Kong soil.
Britain hands Hong Kong back to China in a midnight ceremony on June 30, ending 156 years of colonial rule.
China's proposal was rejected by British Foreign Office spokesman in Hong Kong, Bill Dickson, who said:
"There is no question of Britain agreeing to the deployment of the main PLA garrison in Hong Kong before July 1.
"Britain is the sovereign power and is responsible for the defence of Hong Kong up to the last stroke of midnight on June 30 and that is when China assumes its sovereignty responsibility."
Ruth Vernon, a spokeswoman for the garrison, told Reuters: "Britain is not agreeing to the deployment of the main PLA Garrison of Hong Kong before July 1."

Zhang, deputy chief and official spokesman of China's Hong Kong mission, the Xinhua News Agency branch, said the 1984 Sino-British handover treaty stipulated the PLA would take over the defence of Hong Kong from midnight on June 30.
He said China and Britain were discussing details such as the size and timing of the main unit to move into Hong Kong.
Earlier, Wen Wei Po blasted Britain for not letting the PLA troops move into Hong Kong early.

"The British forces believe it will take them two or three hours to complete their withdrawal from Hong Kong (at the time of the handover). But it refuses to let the PLA move into their barracks early. This is unfair," Wen Wei Po said.
Britain's last garrison members are flying out of Hong Kong -- in civilian clothes -- three hours after the handover on a chartered jumbo jet.
